clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 50s with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented with a 1-week prodrome of fever, nausea, vomiting, and generalized weakness, followed by confusion, back pain, urinary hesitancy, and lower extremity numbness and weakness. On presentation, he was febrile (38.9°C), disoriented, and had 4+/5 strength in hip and knee flexors with ankle clonus and upgoing toes bilaterally. MRI brain showed diffuse leptomeningitis with linear radial perivascular enhancement surrounding the lateral ventricles. Initial MRI thoracic/lumbar spine was normal but showed subtle contrast enhancement of leptomeninges surrounding the conus. CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (85-501/mm³, 87% lymphocytes), elevated protein (306 mg/dL), normal glucose, and normal LDH. Extensive infectious workup (MTB, HIV, syphilis, fungal, viral, Lyme, West Nile) and standard autoimmune markers (oligoclonal bands, ACE, AQP4, MOG) were negative. Meningeal and brain biopsy was performed due to rapidly progressive disease despite broad antimicrobial coverage (vancomycin, ceftriaxone, metronidazole, acyclovir, fluconazole, RIPE, and dexamethasone initiated on admission). Pulse methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily for 5 days followed by solumedrol 60 mg IV daily halted further clinical decline. Repeat spine imaging 11 days after treatment initiation showed longitudinally extensive patchy T2 hyperintense signal in cervical and thoracic spine. Mayo Clinic CSF autoimmune encephalitis panel returned positive for GFAP antibodies at 1:128 (reference <1:2) several days after pulse steroids were initiated. Antimicrobials were discontinued and the patient underwent five sessions of plasmapheresis. At 3-month follow-up, he was ambulating with a cane with full strength except for 4+/5 strength in hip flexors bilaterally, demonstrating significant neurological recovery.

final.trajectory_summary: A man in his 50s with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented with a 1-week prodrome of fever, nausea, vomiting, and generalized weakness, followed by confusion, back pain, urinary hesitancy, and lower extremity numbness and weakness. On presentation, he was febrile (38.9°C), disoriented, and had 4+/5 strength in hip and knee flexors with ankle clonus and upgoing toes bilaterally. MRI brain showed diffuse leptomeningitis with linear radial perivascular enhancement surrounding the lateral ventricles. Initial MRI thoracic/lumbar spine was normal but showed subtle contrast enhancement of leptomeninges surrounding the conus. CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (85-501/mm³, 87% lymphocytes), elevated protein (306 mg/dL), normal glucose, and normal LDH. Extensive infectious workup (MTB, HIV, syphilis, fungal, viral, Lyme, West Nile) and standard autoimmune markers (oligoclonal bands, ACE, AQP4, MOG) were negative. Meningeal and brain biopsy was performed due to rapidly progressive disease despite broad antimicrobial coverage (vancomycin, ceftriaxone, metronidazole, acyclovir, fluconazole, RIPE, and dexamethasone initiated on admission). Pulse methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily for 5 days followed by solumedrol 60 mg IV daily halted further clinical decline. Repeat spine imaging 11 days after treatment initiation showed longitudinally extensive patchy T2 hyperintense signal in cervical and thoracic spine. Mayo Clinic CSF autoimmune encephalitis panel returned positive for GFAP antibodies at 1:128 (reference <1:2) several days after pulse steroids were initiated. Antimicrobials were discontinued and the patient underwent five sessions of plasmapheresis. At 3-month follow-up, he was ambulating with a cane with full strength except for 4+/5 strength in hip flexors bilaterally, demonstrating significant neurological recovery.
